rationale: Evidence from iteration 9 (score 839.6, below the iteration-8 best of 859.0). Raising base_speed from 1.1 to 1.25 turned the slalom timeouts into finishes at the cost of off-track exits: slalom finished 11/20 (vs 12/20), off-track rose from 1 to 7, timeouts fell from 7 to 2, and mean slalom max_error rose to 0.042. Oval (938.8, 20/20) and s-bend (923.7, 20/20) are stable. So speed is no longer the only limit on the slalom: at 1.25 the robot overshoots and leaves the tape, while at 1.1 it runs out of time. The best operating point lies between them. Plan: set base_speed to 1.18 (about halfway between the two tested speeds) and raise kd from 1.8 to 2.0 to add damping against the larger swings that the higher speed produces. The s-bend control effort (about 10) and line-loss events (about 1 per run) are the main risk, and extra kd should help them. Geometry is unchanged (sensors at y=0.08, x=+/-0.04 at 0.02 spacing, size 0.016, track 0.11, body 0.12 x 0.18, mass 0.5, wheel radius 0.03), and kp 2.0, ki 0 and last_direction line loss are unchanged, so any shift is attributable to speed and kd. Expected result: slalom finished count 14 to 17 of 20 and mean slalom time under 2.9 s, with oval and s-bend still near 20/20, for a score of about 870 to 900. Hypotheses: H1, the slalom now fails on a mix of timeouts and off-track exits, and a speed near 1.18 balances them. H2, kd 2.0 reduces slalom max_error and s-bend line-loss events without slowing the robot enough to cause timeouts. Next measurements: slalom finished count, ended_by split (timeout vs off_track), slalom completion_time and max_error, and s-bend line_loss_events, max_error and control_effort. If slalom off-track exits still dominate, the next step is a higher kd (about 2.3) at the same speed. If timeouts dominate, the next step is base_speed 1.22.
